As LLMs became popular, people realized that to have them answer questions about our documents, we needed a good way to store and search through those documents. That made [vector databases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_database), the technology that enabled this, extremely popular.

Then people started getting 6-figure bills for storing motivational quotes their mom had sent them. So we realized we needed to make this process cheaper and faster^[or cut all ties with our moms].

[AI labs](https://openai.com/index/new-embedding-models-and-api-updates/) [stepped in](https://docs.cohere.com/changelog/embed-multimodal-v4) with a technique called [Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13147), which lets you use fewer embedding dimensions without sacrificing much accuracy in your retrieval. Since then, we've more or less lived happily, with smaller vector database bills and faster queries.

Last week I read Doug Turnbull's [article](https://softwaredoug.com/blog/2026/07/24/pca-shrink-ray) about using [Principal Component Analysis (PCA)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.1100)–an older, battle-tested technique–to reduce vector dimensions. And I was curious to see how PCA would perform against MRL.

So I ran an experiment comparing both methods across eight standard retrieval-quality datasets. In this article, I share what I found.

All the code and data is available on [GitHub](https://github.com/dylanjcastillo/blog/tree/main/_extras/matryoshka-vs-pca).

## What are MRL and PCA?

Both methods produce smaller vectors that behave almost like the full ones. But they get there in different ways. 

**MRL** works during training. You train the model with the loss applied at several prefix lengths at once: the first 64 dimensions, the first 128, and so on. This teaches it to pack the most important information at the start of the vector, like a set of nested matryoshka dolls. 

At inference time, you simply keep the first _d_ dimensions and re-normalize the resulting vector. Many modern embedding models are trained this way, but older models aren't, so MRL-based truncation is not available for many popular embedding models.

**PCA** works after training, which means it can be used with any model. You take a sample of embeddings, find the directions along which they vary the most, and keep the top _d_ of them as a projection matrix^[this [page](https://setosa.io/ev/principal-component-analysis/) explains it quite well]. From then on, every document and query gets multiplied by that matrix (and re-normalized) before it goes into the index. 

But you get additional operational complexity. You need to store and version the PCA transformation, then apply the same version consistently when adding to and querying the index. 

## How I ran the experiment

The idea behind the experiment was simple: I would shrink the embeddings with each method, run the benchmarks, and see how much retrieval quality suffers at each size.

I generated all embeddings through OpenRouter and evaluated retrieval on eight [BEIR](https://github.com/beir-cellar/beir) datasets: SciFact, NFCorpus, ArguAna, FiQA, SciDocs, Quora, TREC-COVID, and Webis-Touché 2020. For each dataset, I reduced the embeddings to 512, 256, 128, 64, and 32 dimensions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Dataset details

| dataset | task | corpus | queries |
|---|---|---|---|
| SciFact | scientific claim verification | 5.2K | 300 |
| NFCorpus | medical search | 3.6K | 323 |
| ArguAna | counterargument retrieval | 8.7K | 1,406 |
| FiQA-2018 | financial question answering | 57K | 648 |
| SciDocs | citation recommendation | 25K | 1,000 |
| Quora | duplicate question retrieval | 523K | 10,000 |
| TREC-COVID | biomedical search (COVID-19) | 171K | 50 |
| Touché 2020 | argument retrieval from web docs | 382K | 49 |
:::

There were three questions I wanted to answer.

#### Q1: which method keeps more retrieval quality as you cut dims?

To answer this, I used OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small`, a 1,536-dimensional, MRL-trained model, and reduced its embeddings in two ways.

With **truncation**, I kept the first _d_ dimensions and re-normalized. This is how you [reduce dimensions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings#reducing-embedding-dimensions) with MRL.

With **in-domain PCA**, I fit PCA on the documents from the same dataset I then searched. This is what you would likely do in production: fit the projection on the corpus you are about to index.

Comparing the two shows which method preserves more retrieval quality as the embeddings get smaller.

#### Q2: Is it just the MRL training?

If PCA does well on `text-embedding-3-small`, that might be because MRL training has already organized the embedding space in a convenient way. To test that, I added `text-embedding-ada-002`, an older 1,536-dimensional model that wasn't trained using MRL, as a control.

I applied in-domain PCA to both models. If PCA retains a similar share of retrieval quality on `text-embedding-3-small` and `text-embedding-ada-002`, that suggests its performance does not depend on MRL training.

#### Q3: Does the fitting data matter?

PCA has to be fit on something. In-domain PCA uses the same corpus that will later be searched, but that is not always convenient. You might instead fit PCA once on whatever data you already have and reuse the projection elsewhere.

To measure the cost of doing that, I compared in-domain PCA with **out-of-domain PCA**. For the out-of-domain version, I fit PCA once on 100,000 MS MARCO passages and reused the same projection on every other dataset. This is the lazy version: fit on whatever data you have at the start and never update it.

## Q1: which method keeps more retrieval quality?

I was surprised to see that PCA beat MRL on all dimensions except 512. And on that, the difference was pretty small.

Each cell below shows how much retrieval quality survives the reduction: NDCG@10 at that dimension divided by NDCG@10 at the full 1,536 dimensions, averaged over the eight datasets. 

This is `text-embedding-3-small`, the MRL-trained model:

| dims | Truncation | PCA (in-domain) |
|---|---|---|
| 512 | 98% | 97% |
| 256 | 94% | 95% |
| 128 | 86% | 90% |
| 64 | 71% | 82% |
| 32 | 46% | 65% |

```{python}
#| echo: false
figures.fig_retention(include_ada=False)
```

At 512 dims both methods don't differ by much. But as you continue reducing dimensions, PCA is clearly better.

The results don't differ much by dataset:

```{python}
#| echo: false
figures.fig_ndcg_by_dim()
```

At the smallest sizes, PCA wins on seven of the eight. The only exception is Quora, where MRL holds up unusually well.

## Q2: is it just the MRL training?

Remember the worry from the setup: maybe PCA only looks this good on `text-embedding-3-small` because MRL training already organized the embedding space in some convenient way. If that were true, PCA on `text-embedding-ada-002`, which never saw MRL training, should be noticeably worse.

For the most part, it isn't. Down to 128 dimensions, in-domain PCA retains nearly the same share of quality on both models; below that, the MRL model holds up a few points better:

  </tbody>
</table>

```{python}
#| echo: false
figures.fig_pca_models()
```

One nuance worth flagging: below 128 dimensions, a gap does open up. PCA on `ada-002` retains 78% at 64 dims and 59% at 32, against 82% and 65% on `text-embedding-3-small`. Part of that could be MRL training making the space friendlier to any compression at extreme ratios, and part could simply be that `text-embedding-3-small` is a newer, better model. I can't separate the two with this experiment. But it doesn't change the practical ranking: even PCA on the non-MRL model beats truncation on the MRL model at those dimensions (59% vs 46% at 32 dims), so the low-dimension gap, whatever causes it, doesn't rescue truncation.

Truncation itself is a different story: on `ada-002` it does a few points worse everywhere (41% vs 46% retained at 32 dims). So MRL training does help truncation, as intended. It just doesn't explain PCA's results.

## Q3: does the fitting data matter?

Compared to MRL, PCA adds an annoying extra step: fitting the projection, and potentially refitting it as your index changes. So I wanted to know what happens if you're lazy: fit PCA once, when you first create the index, and never touch it again.

**Out-of-domain fit.** The PCA fit on 100k generic MS MARCO passages performs within a point or two of the in-domain fit everywhere, and on several datasets (ArguAna, NFCorpus) it is actually better (no idea why!): 

```{python}
#| echo: false
figures.fig_ood_gap()
```

**Fit-sample size.** On FiQA (57k docs), PCA fit on a random 1,000 documents matches PCA fit on the full corpus at every dimension. So it seems that for in-domain PCA, the amount of data used for the fitting doesn't impact much. 

```{python}
#| echo: false
figures.fig_fit_size()
```

## What about quantization?

You can also shrink vectors through a method called quantization. In it, you store each dimension with fewer bits: int8 uses 1 byte per dimension (4x smaller than float32), and binary keeps just the sign bit (32x smaller). For the binary results below, both document and query vectors are binarized and compared using the dot product, which is equivalent to ranking by Hamming distance.

Using quantization alone, you get these results at full 1,536 dimensions:

| config | bytes per vector | size vs full float32 | quality retained |
|---|---|---|---|
| int8 | 1,536 | 25% | 100% |
| binary | 192 | 3.1% | 95% |

You can take it further and combine quantization and truncation or PCA, and get some extreme size reduction with just a moderate reduction in quality. 

Using binary quantization and PCA with 521 dimensions lets you keep 87% of the performance, while reducing the raw vector size to 1% of the original. That seems a bit too optimistic, so it might just be my AI psychosis. Take a look at the [results](https://github.com/dylanjcastillo/blog/tree/main/_extras/matryoshka-vs-pca/data/analysis/openai__text-embedding-3-small/quantization_summary.csv) yourself.

## How much can you save? 

I used Weaviate's [pricing calculator](https://weaviate.io/pricing) to estimate the potential savings of reducing vector dimensions. I calculated the price difference for 50M objects on the Flex plan using a Performance Optimized profile:

- 1536 dims: **$12,750/month**
- 128 dims: **$1,173/month**

In a year, this results in savings of ~$140k while theoretically retaining 90% of the quality if you go with PCA or 86% if you go with MRL. If you go with PCA, you'll need to account for the additional operational complexity and costs due to the PCA model. 

## Limitations

- **Corpus size**: I excluded the largest BEIR datasets to keep the budget under control (~$25 spent), so it's possible PCA falls behind MRL at a scale I didn't reach.
- **Not a production setup**: my evaluation runs exact search over raw vectors, which is not how an actual vector database works. A real deployment would use an approximate index, apply its own compression, rescore with full-precision vectors, and often mix in BM25 and a reranker.
- **Benchmark contamination**: BEIR datasets are widely used to train embedding models, so the absolute scores are probably inflated.
